‘This marriage is entirely right. At first I thought otherwise, but now I acknowledge it. The gods fashioned Sibyl Vane for you. Without her you could never have been complete.’

‘Thank you, Basil,’ Dorian Gray replied, clasping his hand. ‘I was sure you would understand. Harry’s cynicism is so great that it frightens me. But the orchestra is beginning. It is perfectly dreadful, though fortunately it lasts only some five minutes. Afterwards the curtain goes up, and you will behold the girl to whom I mean to give my whole life, to whom I have already given every good thing within me.’

Fifteen minutes later, amid a remarkable tumult of applause, Sibyl Vane appeared upon the stage. Yes, she was unquestionably beautiful—among the loveliest beings, Lord Henry reflected, that he had ever beheld. Her timid grace and startled eyes had something of a fawn about them. As she looked upon the crowded, enthusiastic audience, a delicate blush touched her cheeks, like a rose’s reflection in a silver mirror. She drew back several steps, and her lips appeared to quiver. Basil Hallward sprang up and applauded. Dorian Gray remained perfectly still, gazing at her like a man dreaming. Lord Henry looked through his glasses and murmured, ‘Charming! How charming!’

The setting was the hall in Capulet’s house. Romeo, dressed as a pilgrim, had arrived with Mercutio and his other companions. The band, poor as it was, played a few measures, and the dancing commenced. Among the awkward actors in their shabby costumes, Sibyl Vane passed like a being belonging to a nobler world. As she danced, her figure swayed as a plant does beneath the water. The lines of her throat were those of a white lily. Her hands might have been fashioned from cool ivory.

And yet a strange languor possessed her. When her gaze fell upon Romeo, she gave no indication of delight. Her few lines—

Good pilgrim, you judge your hand too harshly, since it shows courteous devotion in this act; saints have hands that pilgrims’ hands may touch, and the meeting of their palms is the holy pilgrims’ kiss—

and the short exchange following them were delivered with complete artificiality. Her voice was exquisite, but its tone rang utterly false. Its colouring was wrong. It drained the verse of all vitality and robbed the passion of reality.

As Dorian Gray watched, his face paled. He felt bewildered and uneasy. Neither friend ventured to address him. To both of them she appeared entirely without ability.

‘What’s wrong?’ Oliver demanded.

‘Quiet!’ said the Dodger. ‘See that old fellow at the bookstall?’

‘The elderly gentleman across the road?’ Oliver asked. ‘Yes, I see him.’

‘He’ll do nicely,’ said the Dodger.

‘An excellent target,’ remarked Master Charley Bates.

Oliver looked in astonishment from one boy to the other, but had no chance to ask any questions. The two slipped across the road and crept up directly behind the old gentleman they had pointed out. Oliver followed for a few steps, then stopped. Unsure whether to move forward or turn back, he watched in silent bewilderment.

The old gentleman looked thoroughly respectable, with powdered hair and gold spectacles. He wore a bottle-green coat with a black velvet collar and white trousers, and had a handsome bamboo cane tucked under his arm. He had picked up a book from the stall and stood reading it as intently as if he were sitting in the armchair in his own study. Indeed, he may well have imagined himself there. His complete absorption made it clear that he noticed neither the bookstall nor the street nor the boys—in fact, nothing except the book. He was reading it straight through, turning each page as he reached its bottom, starting at the first line of the next, and continuing steadily with the keenest interest and eagerness.

Imagine Oliver’s horror and alarm as he stood a few steps away, his eyes open as wide as they could go, and watched the Dodger thrust his hand into the old gentleman’s pocket and pull out a handkerchief! Then he saw him pass it to Charley Bates, and finally watched them both race round the corner at full speed!

In that instant the entire mystery of the handkerchiefs, the watches, the jewels, and the Jew burst upon the boy’s understanding.

For a moment he stood still, terror sending the blood tingling through every vein until he felt as though he were standing in a blazing fire. Then, bewildered and frightened, he fled. Hardly knowing what he was doing, he ran as fast as his feet could carry him.

All this happened within a minute. At the very moment Oliver started running, the old gentleman reached into his pocket, discovered his handkerchief missing, and spun round. Seeing the boy speeding away, he naturally assumed that Oliver had stolen it. Shouting ‘Stop thief!’ at the top of his voice, he set off in pursuit, still holding the book.

‘Yes, burglar’s tools. You seem mighty relieved about that. But what frightened you so? What did you think we’d found?’

Huck was trapped. The old man’s questioning eyes were fixed on him, and he would have given anything for a believable answer. Nothing came to mind. That searching gaze seemed to bore deeper and deeper. A foolish answer occurred to him, and there was no time to consider it. He took a chance and said weakly:

‘Sunday-school books, maybe.’

Poor Huck was too upset even to smile, but the old man burst into a loud, delighted laugh that shook him from head to foot. At last he declared that a laugh like that was money saved, because it did wonders for keeping down the doctor’s bill. Then he added:

‘Poor fellow, you’re pale and worn out. You’re not well at all, so no wonder you’re a bit confused and unsettled. But you’ll recover. Some rest and sleep will put you right again, I hope.’

Huck was annoyed with himself for acting so foolishly and showing such suspicious excitement. After hearing the conversation at the widow’s stile, he had given up the idea that the parcel carried from the tavern contained the treasure. Still, he had only believed it was not the treasure; he had not known for certain. That was why hearing about a bundle being captured had made him lose his composure. On the whole, though, he was glad this little incident had happened. Now he knew beyond any doubt that their bundle was not the bundle he cared about, and the knowledge left him peaceful and wonderfully comfortable. Everything seemed to be working out exactly as it should. The treasure must still be in No. 2; the men would be caught and put in jail that day; and he and Tom could collect the gold that night without difficulty or fear of anyone interrupting them.

Just as they finished breakfast, someone knocked at the door. Huck sprang into hiding. He had no wish to be connected, even remotely, with what had happened. The Welshman let in several ladies and gentlemen, including the Widow Douglas. He also noticed groups of townspeople climbing the hill to stare at the stile. Clearly the news had spread. He had to tell his visitors the story of the night, and the widow warmly expressed her gratitude for being saved.

‘Don’t mention it, madam. There’s someone else you may owe more to than you owe me and my boys, but he won’t let me give his name. We’d never have been there without him.’
